test: assert_* macros formatting features are hard to use

## Version
```
└── tokio-test v0.2.0-alpha.1
    ├── tokio-executor v0.2.0-alpha.1 (*)
    ├── tokio-io v0.2.0-alpha.1 (*)
    ├── tokio-sync v0.2.0-alpha.1 (*)
    └── tokio-timer v0.3.0-alpha.1 (*)
```

## Platform

Linux pop-os 5.0.0-23-generic #24~18.04.1-Ubuntu SMP Mon Jul 29 16:12:28 UTC 2019 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

## Subcrates

test

## Description

I was unable to actually utilize the advertised custom message feature of the `assert_*`  macros to take arbitrary formatting arguments.  Attempting to call them like so:

```rust
use tokio_test::{assert_pending, task::MockTask};

struct SomeFuture;
impl Future for SomeFuture {
    type Output = ();

    fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context) -> Poll<Self::Output> {
        Poll::Ready(())
    }
}
impl Unpin for SomeFuture {}

#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyData;

#[test]
fn test_msg() {
    let mut task = MockTask::new();
    assert_pending!(task.poll(&mut SomeFuture), "custom-msg {:?}", MyData);
}
```

I expected this to both compile and when running tests to fail the `test_msg` test with this  message: 
```
thread 'test_msg' panicked at 'ready; value = (); custom-msg MyData', src/lib.rs:19:5
```

Instead, it fails to compile with this error message:

```
error[E0716]: temporary value dropped while borrowed
  --> src/lib.rs:19:49
   |
19 |     assert_pending!(task.poll(&mut SomeFuture), "custom-msg {:?}", MyData);
   |     --------------------------------------------^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^----------
   |     |                                           |
   |     |                                           creates a temporary which is freed while still in use
   |     temporary value is freed at the end of this statement
   |     borrow later used here
```

I cannot figure out how to use the custom formatting arguments correctly without this happening.

Also, I think the ergonomics of using the `tt` macro pattern type for the formatting arguments is quite poor, since I believe this means that many simple expressions would need to be wrapped in an explicit set of braces.  For instance, an `Enum::Variant` is not a single `tt`.  I believe it would be simpler to have the formatting elements be of pattern type `expr` would lead to the expected semantics of being able to use arbitrary expressions as formatting arguments.

```
│   │   ├── tokio v1.26.0 (*)

│   ├── tokio v1.26.0 (*)
│   └── tokio-util v0.7.7 (*)
└── tokio v1.26.0 (*)
```

**Platform**
Linux

**Description**
The following will fail intermittently (a simplification of https://github.com/taskcluster/taskcluster/issues/6280). It fails particularly under high CPU load.

```rust
use std::error::Error;
use tempfile::tempfile;
use tokio::io::{copy, File};

const DATA: &[u8] = b"HELLO/WORLD";

#[tokio::test]
async fn t() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut file: File = tempfile()?.into();
    file.write_all(DATA).await?;
    let mut file2 = file.try_clone().await?;
    let mut buf = Cursor::new(Vec::new());
    copy(&mut file2, &mut buf).await?;
    assert_eq!(writer.into_inner(), DATA);
}
```

What's happening is that the `write_all` is starting a write operation in another thread, and returning Poll::Ready. The `try_clone`, however, misses that there's an operation ongoing and creates a new File with no such operation. So there's a race between that `write` completing in another thread and the `read` performed by `copy`.

I would expect the `try_clone` to wait until any operations that have already been described as complete actually are complete. I can see that being hard to implement, though. Perhaps the documentation could be updated with something like

> **NOTE**
> Ongoing operations on the source File may not be complete when it is cloned. New operations on the cloned File may "race" with these ongoing operations.

This is similar to https://github.com/tokio-rs/tokio/issues/4796. I couldn't find how that issue was fixed (no commits around June 30, 2022 seemed relevant), but the current documentation doesn't describe this situation (at least not in a way that's clear to me even after having found the problem).

In `block_in_place`, deferred wakers are woken up after the blocking call and not before

**Version**
1.49

**Description**
I could be missing something, but it seems that when `block_in_place` is called, deferred wakers are woken up after the blocking call finishes and not before.
This may lead to indefinite stalling in (relatively) innocent-looking code.

E.g. consider there is task1 like this:
```
let (action_tx, action_rx) = mpsc::unbounded_channel();
...
loop {
    select! {
        Some(action) = action_rx.recv() => {
            do stuff and send back the result via a one-shot channel that is part of `action`
        }
        ...
    }
}
```
and there is task2 that sends an action to task1 and waits for the result using `block_in_place`.

What may happen (e.g. under heavy load) is:
1) task1's budget gets exhausted, so the `select!`'s future returns `Pending` and the waker is deferred.
2) the last time that task1's action channel was checked, it was non-empty, so no waker was registered by the channel itself.
3) task2 switches to the same thread that task1 is on.
4) task2 sends an action to task1 and uses `block_in_place` to wait for the result. However there is no way for task1 to be woken up before `block_in_place` finishes.

```rust
#[tokio::main]
```

```rust
    let variable = "";

}
```

The spans of `variable;` point to `tokio::runtime::Builder::new_multi_thread()` in the output of the macro. This causes rust-analyzer to (correctly) highlight `variable` as a function call and to show the `new_multi_thread` function on hover.

Debug impl of mpsc::error::TrySendError<T> should not bound T: Debug

Hi.

### Context
I am writing some kind of generic library code and would like to impose as little as possible bounds to the user.
I am using **bounded mpsc channels** and and in some place of the code I needed to call `try_send(T)` and since it has to work there it's the perfect example of where to use an `.expect("channel has capacity")` to panic in case it doesn't work.

Now, the `expect` method on `Result<T, E>` requires `E: fmt::Debug`, and in this case, `E` is `TrySendError<T>` which implement `Debug` with a derive macro and thus requires my user data to implement `Debug` on its data type.

### **Describe the solution you'd like**
Manual `impl<T> Debug for TrySendError<T>` instead of the derive macro that expands to `impl<T: Debug> Debug for TrySendError<T>`.

### **Describe alternatives you've considered**
When lookin at the **std library, on the mpsc channel** too, there is also a [`try_send(T)` method ](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/mpsc/struct.SyncSender.html#method.try_send) and the error, [TrySendError\<T\>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/mpsc/enum.TrySendError.html) implement `Debug` without any bound on `T` ([see here](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/mpsc/enum.TrySendError.html#impl-Debug-for-TrySendError%3CT%3E)). 

### **Additional context**
It would also be more uniform with the std library API.

### **Workaround**
For now the workaround I am using is [`try_reserve`](https://docs.rs/tokio/latest/tokio/sync/mpsc/struct.Sender.html#method.try_reserve) instead of `try_send`. 
Underneath it is almost the same code except it returns an `Ok(Permit)` or `Err(TrySendError<()>)` (and `()` impl Debug)
So I can use `.except(...)` on this result, I just the extra step to actually send on the permit, but it doesn't fail ever.

max_blocking_threads documentation should perhaps indicate that Tokio internally uses those too

**Version**

1.25.0

**Platform**

Windows, any version

**Description**

As written, the documentation for max_blocking_threads suggests it's only used for

This probably warrants a small disclaimer that setting this low-ish may be a good idea. In particular, on Windows, reading a pipe is a blocking read and will take away a blocking thread forever.

If you set `max_blocking_threads` to a low value (e.g. in our case, in a test, we were setting it to 2), you can easily find yourself in a situation where `spawn_blocking` just hangs forever, because all your blocking threads are waiting on a pair of idle pipes (stdout and stderr of a child process, in our case), which might be rather unexpected!

rt: consider having `runtime::Builder` panic if setting `global_queue_interval` to zero

Setting it to `1` has the effect of inverting the order in which the multi-threaded runtime checks the global queue. This is probably not the intended behavior.

Setting it to `0` panics with an 'attempt to calculate the remainder with a divisor of zero' error.
